candidates_tested.description: how fast the escalated amount was reached (max_amount / days to escalate) - a patient ring and a fast-strike ring look different here even at the same amount
combined device+address sharing count - a stronger single ring signal than either alone
purchase count relative to time - flags accounts that transact unusually rapidly before escalating
1 only if BOTH device and address are shared - isolates coordinated rings from incidental single-signal overlap (e.g. a shared household address only)
time between account creation and the first purchase - a long dormant period before any activity is itself a pattern

autopsy.failure_type: recall drift from untested fast‑strike rings
autopsy.root_cause: The deployed rule only triggers when max_amount > 7,964 and time_to_escalation > 7 days. The attacker search never sampled time_to_escalation below 10 days, so the model never saw fast‑strike behavior, causing recall to collapse as real rings move to shorter escalation times. The drift monitor confirms this gap.
autopsy.existing_control_failure: Because the policy relies on a high time_to_escalation threshold, it fails to flag rings that act quickly, even when other risk signals are strong.

hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Because fast‑strike rings use high amounts in short bursts, adding amount_velocity and ring_density alongside max_amount and escalation_ratio will detect these attacks that the current high‑time threshold overlooks.
